questions.q: Why does this lesson say an exact numeric match between your reproduction and the paper's reported result is actually the LESS likely outcome of an honest attempt?
options: Because exact matches are only possible with proprietary hardware
Because of hardware drift, specification gaps, and the reproducibility-vs-replicability distinction already covered in this chapter
Because published papers usually contain fabricated numbers
Because quantum circuits cannot be reproduced under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties this to the chapter's earlier lessons: hardware drift, the near-universal specification gap, and the difference between reproducing original code vs. independently replicating a method all make an exact match the less likely outcome.

questions.q: What is the first step in this lesson's diagnostic checklist for a discrepancy, and why does it come first?
options: Re-running the experiment on a completely different device
Concluding the published paper's claim is wrong
Contacting the paper's authors immediately
Checking your own implementation for bugs -- the most common source of discrepancy, and cheapest to check
questions.explain: The lesson lists implementation bugs first specifically because they are the most common source of discrepancy and the cheapest to check, before moving on to parameter mismatches, specification gaps, hardware differences, and statistical noise.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against interpreting a mismatch as 'I found a flaw in a published paper' too quickly?
options: Because the far more common reality is a bug or parameter mismatch in your own implementation, which must be ruled out first
Because only the paper's original authors are permitted to find flaws in their own work
Because published papers are never allowed to be challenged
Because finding a flaw in a paper is always impossible
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a basic research-integrity matter: treating your own code as the most likely error source, and only escalating the claim after genuinely ruling it out, avoids the specific failure mode of overclaiming a flaw that was actually your own bug.

questions.q: In the worked GHZ example, what was the actual source of the measured discrepancy?
options: Statistical noise alone fully explained the gap
The student used linear extrapolation instead of the paper's specified Richardson extrapolation -- a missed detail from the appendix
The paper's claim was proven false on larger hardware
The student used the wrong number of qubits in the circuit
questions.explain: The worked example traces the discrepancy to a missed extraction detail -- using linear instead of the paper's specified Richardson extrapolation -- which, once corrected, closed most of the gap.

questions.q: If a measured discrepancy falls well within the overlapping confidence intervals of both your result and the paper's result, what does this lesson's checklist say that indicates?
options: Confidence intervals are irrelevant to evaluating discrepancies
The apparent difference may just be statistical noise, not a real discrepancy requiring further diagnosis
This always means your implementation has a bug
This is definitive proof the paper's claim is false
questions.explain: The checklist's step 5 (statistical noise) explicitly covers this: an apparent difference with wide, overlapping confidence intervals may not be a real discrepancy at all, given the shot count used.
